analysis.one_liner: Requires data centers and other giant power users to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades built for them.
analysis.headline: The Data Center Fair Share Act was introduced in September 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to two House committees; no hearing, vote, or further action has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: When a data center needs 100 megawatts or more of electricity, utilities typically build new power plants and transmission lines for it, and the costs get spread across all customers on the electric bill. This bill would change federal utility law so those large customers pay the full cost of the upgrades made just for them, even if they later cancel their contract. States would have to consider and adopt this rule, and any state that did not would lose 100% of its federal highway money.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential and small-business electricity customers, especially in states like Virginia where data centers are driving up demand for new power plants and transmission lines. Today, utilities recover the cost of those upgrades from everyone's bill; the bill would make the data centers that cause the cost pay it directly, and would keep charging them even if they shut down and leave the upgrades behind.

how_it_helps.text: Requires electric rates for large-load customers (non-residential customers with 100 megawatts or more of peak demand at a single site or campus) to recover the full, incremental costs of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade needed to serve them [S2].
Keeps charging those costs to the large customer even if the customer terminates its contract or stops buying power, so ratepayers are not left paying for abandoned infrastructure [S2].

Requires utilities, before building an upgrade for a large-load customer, to either get a contribution in aid of construction covering the full cost or assign the full cost to the class of large-load customers [S2].

Directs every state regulator and nonregulated utility to open proceedings within one year and decide within two years whether to adopt the standard, and withholds 100% of a state's federal highway apportionment if it does not [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data center operators — including the cloud and AI companies behind them — would pay the full price of power infrastructure built for their facilities, instead of sharing it with everyone's electric bill. States that refuse to adopt the standard would forfeit their entire federal highway allotment, and some of the added cost to data centers could eventually show up in prices for cloud and AI services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data center operators; noncompliant states' highway funds

drawbacks.text: The penalty is extreme: a state that does not adopt the standard loses 100% of its federal highway apportionment, not a partial share, which gives states essentially no middle ground and could pull federal road money away from residents over a utility-ratemaking dispute [S2].

The bill sets a federal ratemaking mandate that overrides state utility commissions' traditional control over who pays for grid upgrades, and pre-exempts states that have already voted on a comparable standard [S2].

Higher, more certain costs for data centers could slow data center construction in some states, and some of those costs would likely be passed through to customers of cloud and AI services in the form of higher prices — general knowledge about cost pass-through, not stated in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — making the customers who cause expensive grid upgrades pay for them rather than spreading the cost across household bills — is straightforward ratepayer protection, and the stranded-cost provision guards against data centers that build, then leave. The weakness is the enforcement tool: threatening to strip a state of its entire federal highway funding over a utility rule is a sledgehammer that could hurt the very residents the bill claims to protect, and the cost shift to data centers will partly resurface in prices for digital services. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs those costs, but the highway-fund provision is badly proportioned.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no cosponsors, hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA) introduced the bill on September 8, 2026 [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, with the Speaker to determine how the bill would be divided between them [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action — appears in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has lost anything and nothing has changed: the status quo continues, which favors data center operators, who keep adding electricity demand under existing rate rules that spread upgrade costs across all customers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — data centers under current rate rules

for.name: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Data Center Fair Share Act and referred it to Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no members beyond the sponsor have taken a position, so no partisan split is visible yet.

industries.industry: Data centers and hyperscale cloud/AI companies
industries.note: They would have to pay the full incremental cost of power plants and transmission lines built for their facilities, including stranded costs if they cancel — costs currently spread across everyone's electric bill. Their interest in the status quo runs directly against household ratepayers who absorb those costs today.

Utilities would lose the option of recovering upgrade costs from the general rate base, but they would still build the infrastructure and collect the revenue — just billed to the large customer instead of everyone. Ratepayers currently footing data-center-driven upgrade costs would see their burden shift.
States that adopt a comparable standard are spared; states that do not lose 100% of federal highway apportionments, which forces a choice between a utility rule and road funding for their residents.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill from a single sponsor with zero cosponsors, split between two committees, very rarely advances. Unless other members — including colleagues from data-center-heavy districts — sign on and the Energy and Commerce Committee schedules a hearing, the bill will likely expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
